name: Operation ledger with micro-journeys
desc: The micro-journey row is excellent, but as a full composition it is subsumed by O-09, which adds geography at no cost. Keep the row and drop this page.
intent: What is every transport doing right now, scannable in one pass?

name: Country as the operation (fullscreen map, attached labels)
desc: Map as landscape wallpaper: about 55% of the screen is sea and Spain, and the labels collide where the operation is densest. The attached-label idea survives elsewhere (O-09, R-07).
intent: Where is everything, and what is attached to each moving object?

name: Day board (temporal, all transports)
desc: The temporal spine for the whole operation. Restriction-as-time-band is a genuinely strong FleetOS idea.
intent: When will each transport do what today, and where do restrictions fall in time?

name: Readiness matrix (transport × check)
desc: Spreadsheet. Facts lose their native form and there is nothing temporal or physical. The glyph vocabulary is worth keeping; the composition is not.
intent: Which transports are blocked, and by which dimension?

name: Latitude schematic (Portugal as a metro line)
desc: Strong, distinctively FleetOS, and native to Portugal's geometry. A candidate replacement for the landscape overview map.
intent: Can the country be straightened so every transport becomes a comparable vertical journey?

name: Accordion instrument (list that opens into the object)
desc: A generic accordion. Expanding one row destroys the comparability that made the list worth having. In-place growth belongs to a transition, not a layout.
intent: Can scanning and inspecting happen in the same place, without leaving the list?

name: Three sentences (attention-only, typographic)
desc: Superb landing sentence, but a workspace can't be built from three sentences. On a calm day it is empty. Use as the attention header above O-09.
intent: If the operator only reads one screen, what must change in the next hour?

name: The yard (fleet as physical silhouettes)
desc: Decorative at population scale. Eight silhouettes look lovely and forty would be wallpaper. The load-fill glyph survives as a row micro-object.
intent: What physical capacity do I have, and where is it committed?

name: Portrait map spine + ledger (no white panel)
desc: Best answer so far to 'map plus list'. The portrait orientation and leader-line binding replace the generic side panel.
intent: Can geography and the dense list coexist without a map-left/panel-right split?

name: Legal buckets under the day
desc: The strongest legality representation. It causally joins activity and rule on one clock. Core FleetOS.
intent: Is the driver legal now and for the rest of the day, and which rule binds first?

name: Week as stacked columns (portrait time)
desc: Good weekly rhythm, but the orientation conflicts with the horizontal temporal spine. Take the gauge, not the rotation.
intent: What is the driver's weekly rhythm, and how much is left?

name: Qualifications as physical cards
desc: The validity axis is strong; the card rendering is borderline decorative. Keep the axis plus a flat document glyph.
intent: Which documents allow this person to drive what, and until when?

name: Driver ⇄ vehicle coupling
desc: Too diagrammatic and static. The monogram stands in for a person, and connector curves carry less information than one sentence would.
intent: Is this person compatible with this exact combination?

name: Legality projected onto the road
desc: Distinctively FleetOS. Answers the dispatcher's real question ('where must he stop?'). A primary Driver+Route primitive.
intent: Where on the road will the driver's legal time run out?

name: Spatial driver: reachable legal corridor
desc: Right semantics at the wrong scale: the 49 km legal remainder is a sliver on a regional map. D-05 says the same thing legibly.
intent: Geographically, how far can the driver legally go before the next mandatory event?

name: Driver history as event spine
desc: A generic activity feed. Equal visual weight for every event buries the one infraction that matters, so it needs significance grouping before it is FleetOS.
intent: What happened with this driver recently, and is there a pattern?

name: Forward assignments (5-day horizon)
desc: Conflict-as-overlap is exactly right, but the composition is sparse and the days compress. Belongs as a zoom level of the Driver temporal spine, not a page.
intent: What is this driver committed to, and where do commitments collide with rest rules?

name: One sentence driver (typography only)
desc: Excellent as an attention header or a lock-screen / mobile glance. Not a workspace by itself.
intent: What is the single most important fact about this driver right now?

name: Driver dossier (documents bound to person)
desc: Too ERP-like. Card/list soup with no native form. Qualifications should be time (D-03 axis) or relation (D-04).
intent: Which documents prove this driver is allowed, and which are stale?

name: Reassignment comparison (two drivers, one transport)
desc: Decision comparison layer done right: native time form, clear recommendation, honest reason. Core primitive.
intent: Who should take this transport, and why?

name: Tachograph disc (circular 24h)
desc: Skeuomorphic, visually strong but operationally unclear. Linear time beats it everywhere.
intent: Can the legacy tachograph disc metaphor carry the driver's day?

name: Annotated technical elevation (facts on the object)
desc: Physical-object-first at its best. Information integrated into the object. Distinctively FleetOS.
intent: What is the state of this combination, read directly off the machine?

name: Load plan as unloading sequence
desc: A strong physical argument for multi-drop only. It overlaps V-01 and the existing lab load plan; fold the unload-order arrows into those.
intent: Is the load arranged in the order it will leave the trailer?

name: Range as a draining band along the road
desc: Correct and honest, but it is a layer of the route axis, not a vehicle view. As its own page it duplicates the route.
intent: Will the fuel reach the next refuelling point, and where should it refuel?

name: Maintenance as component lifelines
desc: Dashboard progress bars by another name. The projected-wear idea should be callouts on the elevation, not a bar stack.
intent: Which service is due, measured in the units each component actually wears in?

name: Trailer comparison (stacked elevations)
desc: Native physical comparison with a clear recommendation, but four elevations eat the screen and cost/distance is buried. Pair candidates with a ranked list instead.
intent: Which free trailer can replace PT-3821, and what differs physically?

name: Clearance portal (truck front vs. structure)
desc: The single most convincing 'physical fact' representation. Anyone understands it in one second. Keep.
intent: Does the vehicle physically fit under this structure?

name: Spatial truck in a lens (position + heading + context)
desc: Visually strong but operationally unclear. A decorative lens with a false-precision risk.
intent: Where exactly is the truck and what is immediately around it?

name: Spec sheet (technical register)
desc: Too ERP-like and too static. Specs should surface only where they cause something (V-06, V-01).
intent: What are the registered characteristics of the vehicle?

name: Truck + route: vehicle constraints along the corridor
desc: Excellent concept (structures as gates against this truck), but the gates cluster at Porto and the labels collide. It works better as a layer of R-03.
intent: Where on the route does this specific vehicle meet a physical constraint?

name: Axle mass diagram (weight as force)
desc: A strong physical idiom, but niche. Belongs inside the truck elevation as an optional layer, not a full view.
intent: Is the mass legal and well-distributed per axle?

name: Combination assembly (tractor · trailer · driver as parts)
desc: An instruction-manual exploded view. Couplings carry no information and part-swap is better done inside V-05.
intent: Which parts make up this transport's equipment and which part is the problem?

name: Journey strip (horizontal, stops as stations)
desc: Necessary but not sufficient: the baseline strip already exists in the lab. Without time or geography it can't show slack or context. A component, not a direction.
intent: Where is the transport in its journey and what comes next?

name: Time–distance diagram (Marey chart)
desc: The most information-dense honest representation of a timed route. A railway-planning idiom that fits trucking perfectly. Distinctive.
intent: Will each stop be reached inside its window, and how much slack is there?

name: Strip map (real corridor, straightened)
desc: Map as corridor, the best synthesis of geography and journey. A primary FleetOS primitive.
intent: Can we keep real geography but give the route the clarity of a linear strip?

name: Side-mounted vertical route + portrait map
desc: Clever N–S alignment, but it breaks for E–W routes and leaves a large empty right column. Keep the alignment trick for portrait layouts only.
intent: Can a vertical route strip sit next to a portrait map so that both share the N–S direction?

name: The console (stacked tracks aligned to km)
desc: Too dense as a default. Excellent as an expert 'all layers' mode where the user adds tracks on demand.
intent: Everything that varies along the route in one aligned instrument.

name: Candidate alternatives (fastest vs. no tolls)
desc: Honest trade-off and a clear recommendation, but half the screen is a map whose only message is 'two lines diverge', and the ledger is a table.
intent: Which route should this transport take, and what does each cost?

name: Fullscreen route map with embedded km axis
desc: Fullscreen landscape again: Spain and the Atlantic take most of the screen. Embedding km ticks in the line is good; this frame is not.
intent: Can the map itself carry the journey's measurements?

name: Local stop focus (site plan)
desc: Decorative: FleetOS has no site-plan data, so this view promises something it can't deliver. Only the arrival-window fragment survives.
intent: What happens at this specific stop: access, dock, window, cargo?

name: Restrictions on route (time-of-day validity on the corridor)
desc: The cleanest 'does the rule hit my transport' picture, but it is the same km×time plane as R-02. Fold restriction rectangles into R-02 rather than a second view.
intent: Which restrictions will this route meet, at the time it will meet them?

name: Itinerary roll (vertical text-first route)
desc: Wrong user. Useful as an export, not a FleetOS workspace composition.
intent: Can the route be read as an itinerary document, like a road book?

name: Route as horizon (perspective road)
desc: Consumer sat-nav, sci-fi adjacent. Visually strong, operationally useless for a dispatcher.
intent: Can a 'driver's-eye' perspective convey what's coming?

name: Causal logic tree (AND of conditions → verdict)
desc: Rules as logic, with honesty about missing facts. The defining restriction primitive. Keep.
intent: Why does (or might) this restriction apply to this transport?

name: Affected segment at street scale (VCI ring)
desc: Real geometry at the right scale, but without a basemap Porto is abstract, and the right column is a conventional side panel.
intent: Exactly which roadway does the restriction cover, and where does our route touch it?

name: Missing fact drawn as a gap in the object
desc: Turns uncertainty into a concrete, physical action. A uniquely FleetOS idea. Keep.
intent: What single fact is missing, where does it physically live, and who can provide it?

name: Transport impact over time (who crosses when)
desc: Restriction-centric population view, temporal and causal. Keep.
intent: Which transports cross the restricted segment, and do their crossings fall inside the validity window?

name: Detour decision on the corridor (two strips)
desc: Two thin strips repeat each other, and the length difference (+69 km) is the only message. A sentence and R-06 do it better.
intent: If a restriction blocks the route, what is the alternative and what does it cost?

name: Evidence & provenance chain
desc: Essential for trust and in correct document form, but it's a rarely-opened page. It should be a fold-out of X-01, not a destination.
intent: Why should I trust this restriction? Where does every part come from?

name: Fullscreen spatial restriction (IP3 works, night)
desc: Fullscreen landscape for a 40 km object: mostly empty land, with time reduced to labels. Spatial restriction mode must be inset or portrait.
intent: Where are the works and how does traffic get around them?

name: Restriction register (list of rules)
desc: Too ERP-like. Restrictions only matter relative to transports (X-04) or space (X-02). Admin-only.
intent: Which restrictions exist in the system?

name: Dossier as fanned paper
desc: Decorative skeuomorph. Fanned overlap hides the very content the dossier exists to show.
intent: What paper exists for this transport, and what state is each sheet in?

name: Revision diff on the document itself
desc: The diff shown in native document form with causal margin notes. Strong and distinctive.
intent: What changed between rev. 6 and rev. 7, and why?

name: Issued document at reading scale + live fields
desc: The canonical document view and the live/frozen distinction are both right, but the generous whitespace and single sheet per screen make it a component rather than a direction.
intent: What exactly did we issue, and which fields are live versus frozen?

name: Version history as a ribbon of thumbnails
desc: The history-ribbon structure is right, but thumbnails at this scale are illegible and only work as recognition glyphs.
intent: How did this document evolve, and which revision was valid when?

name: Reissue proposal (cause → document → consequence)
desc: Cause → document → consequence is exactly the question, but the three-column arrow flow reads as a process diagram. Integrate the consequence list into F-02's margin.
intent: Something changed in the transport. Do I need to reissue, and what happens if I do?

name: Document vs. live transport (mismatch audit)
desc: Strong check, generic form. Better as highlights directly on the sheet (F-03 plus F-05 markings).
intent: Does the paper still match reality?

name: Document + related entities (relation map)
desc: Graph-as-decoration. The relations are better expressed as linked fields on the sheet (F-03).
intent: Who and what does this document bind together?

name: Qualification document against the transport calendar
desc: The projection-onto-calendar idea is valuable but belongs in the Driver forward view (D-08), not as a document page.
intent: Will this person's qualification document still be valid for every transport they're planned on?

name: Lab base: ranked situations + map tile
desc: The ranking logic is right. The composition is the generic split this exploration should leave behind; O-07 + O-09 do it better.
intent: What needs me now (lab landing)?

name: Lab: all drivers' day ribbons
desc: A strong temporal spine with the wrong neighbour. Put the D-01 legal bands into the rows and drop the tile.
intent: How is every driver's day shaping up?

name: Lab: driver legality counters
desc: Superseded by D-01, where the same counters live on the activity clock and the binding limit is visible.
intent: Is the driver legal?

name: Lab: 'Pausa obrigatória até 10:50'
desc: The best existing Driver state, but it is still a page with panels. The headline + ribbon should survive into D-01/D-05.
intent: What must this driver do next?

name: Lab: driver spatial mode (map + white panel)
desc: The exact 'white cards on map' pattern the brief warns against.
intent: Where is the driver on the map?

name: Lab: 'Um facto da viatura decide a VCI'
desc: The strongest state already in the lab, and the seed of V-01, X-03 and V-06.
intent: Which vehicle fact decides this restriction?

name: Lab: vehicle load (elevation + top plan)
desc: The drawing is a keeper; the surrounding page is not. Drop the tile and the readings row.
intent: How is the trailer loaded?

name: Lab: choose trailer (table of candidates)
desc: ERP-like. V-05's stacked elevations with a marked recommendation answer the same question physically.
intent: Which trailer replaces the current one?

name: Lab: route layers + stops table + map
desc: Right ingredients, overloaded composition. Splitting into R-02 (time) + R-03 (corridor) is cleaner.
intent: Where should the pause be, along the route?

name: Lab: documents dossier (3 columns + sheet preview)
desc: Correct content, wrong hierarchy: F-02/F-03 give the sheet the stage and move the diff onto it.
intent: Is the paperwork consistent with the transport?

name: Lab: restriction applicability (facts + logic + map)
desc: Good honesty, weak logic form. X-01's wiring and X-02's scale are the upgrade.
intent: Does this restriction apply, and what is unknown?

name: Lab: transport overview (journey + Iberia map)
desc: Map as decoration, the clearest example in the lab. The journey strip survives (R-01).
intent: What is this transport's whole state?

name: Lab: restrictions × transports (multi-lens list)
desc: X-04 answers this question as time, in a fraction of the ink.
intent: Which restrictions affect which transports?

name: Lab: map-dominant vehicle + restriction logic
desc: Spatial mode should be portrait/corridor (O-09, R-03); the panel logic belongs to X-01.
intent: Where is the vehicle going and what restriction lies ahead?

name: Docking seam
desc: The job and the driver are two halves that have to lock together. Every compatibility check is a joint on the seam, and the one that fails is a broken notch.

name: Magnetic field of candidates
desc: The job sits like a magnet. Each driver is placed by distance to pickup (x) and legal hours left (y), and the pull lines thicken with fit. The best candidate is pulled hardest.

name: Legal envelope around the trajectory
desc: The job's plan is a line in time × distance. The driver's legality is a shaded envelope of reachable states. Where the line touches the envelope edge is where the driver has to stop.

name: Editorial assignment spread
desc: The assignment as a magazine spread: giant names locked together by a ×, with the facts set as editorial columns. Pure typographic confidence.

name: Blueprint cutaway, cargo dropping in
desc: A dark blueprint of the combination with the job's cargo falling into its slots, numbered by unload order. Weight and space fill visibly. Dribbble's hero-object energy, held in FleetOS ink.

name: Filmstrip: the truck at every stop
desc: The same truck drawn four times along the corridor, once per stop. Load, fuel and mass change between frames, so you read the job as a physical sequence.

name: Stencil overlay
desc: The job's requirements are drawn as a dashed stencil (minimum length, height, axles). Candidate trucks are overlaid on it in thin ink, and whatever overflows or falls short shows as positive or negative space.

name: The week is a trailer
desc: A truck's week drawn as one long trailer deck. Jobs are cargo blocks occupying time slots, empty deck is idle capacity, and the workshop slot is hatched. Utilisation becomes a load plan.

name: Exploded isometric wallet
desc: The driver's documents as stacked isometric plates. The expiring CQM lifts off the stack and casts its consequence (the transports it will block) onto the floor.

name: Validity skyline (whole team)
desc: Each driver is a building. Its floors are documents and the height is days of validity left. The planning horizon is a horizontal line: anything below it is a problem in waiting.

name: Documents hanging by threads into the day
desc: The driver's day runs below. Documents hang above it on threads that touch exactly the moments they're used: the tacho card on every driving block, the CMR on each stop.

name: Documents clipped to the machine
desc: Each document is a paper tag clipped to the part it certifies: IPO on the chassis, insurance on the cab, tacho calibration on the dashboard, CMR on the rear doors. Expired tags flap red.

name: Paper signposts along the road
desc: Documents stand on the corridor like roadside signposts at the km where they get stamped. Signed ones are solid, pending ones are outlined, and the CMR changes revision mid-road.

name: The plate as the hero
desc: The registration plate set enormous as the identity of the machine, with every document orbiting it at a distance proportional to days of validity left. Closer means more urgent.

name: Gate run (front elevations in sequence)
desc: The truck's front profile passes through every physical gate on the route, left to right in km order. Margins are tight negative spaces, and the unknown gate is drawn in dashed outline.

name: Envelope chart (height × mass)
desc: Every restriction becomes a forbidden region on a physical plane. The combination is a point with an uncertainty bar where data is missing. Legal = the white space the point sits in.

name: Night operations map (dark, portrait)
desc: A dark-mode, portrait, Portugal-native map for night monitoring. Restrictions are muted embers with their active hours, and the truck carries its next restriction as a label. Calm, not neon.

name: Rule plates over the machine
desc: Road-sign plates are drawn at scale over the parts of the truck they judge: a height bar over the roof, a mass disc over the axles, an axle-height ruler at the front wheel. The rule and the object share one drawing.

name: Skewer: stacked planes, pinned facts
desc: Job, Route, Truck, Driver, Documents and Restriction are isometric planes stacked like acetate sheets. A single fact (the VCI crossing at 15:05) is a pin piercing every plane it touches, so the cross-domain relation becomes literal.

name: Constellation on portrait Portugal
desc: The whole operation as a constellation placed geographically. Each node is a tiny physical glyph (truck, person, sheet, sign), and fine arcs bind what belongs together. The selected cluster is lit; the rest stays dim.

name: Commitment flows (drivers → jobs → trucks)
desc: A Sankey of the day: driver hours flow into jobs, and jobs flow into trucks. Ribbon width is hours committed. Unassigned jobs are dangling ribbons and idle resources are stubs.

name: Departures board (split-flap, on paper)
desc: An industrial split-flap board: each row is a job with driver, truck, document and restriction cells that flip when state changes. It's a dynamic, readable-from-across-the-room ops wall, inked on paper rather than glowing.

name: Relation lens (rings of distance)
desc: J-4217 at the centre. Ring 1 holds what it physically uses, ring 2 the papers and stops, ring 3 the rules and other jobs competing for the same resources. Distance encodes how directly something affects the job.

name: Editorial dossier spread (Awwwards energy)
desc: J-4217 laid out as a magazine spread: a giant km numeral, the truck drawing bleeding off the page, pull-quote decisions and a caption-sized ledger. Premium editorial pacing applied to operations.

name: Threads draw into the day
desc: The threads unspool from each document and land on the moments they touch, staggered. The eye learns the relation as the sequence plays.

name: Magnetic pull settles
desc: The candidates fade in and the pull lines draw from the job outward. The strongest pull completes first and the rest follow by fit, so the ranking is felt before it is read.

name: Skewer assembles
desc: The planes drop into the stack one by one, then the pin pierces all six. The relation is literally assembled in front of the operator.

name: Truck rides the corridor
desc: The truck glides along the unrolled corridor while the fuel and legal gauges drain and reset at Santarém. It's dynamism carrying meaning: the pause is visibly the moment both refill.

name: Normal transport (map as 25% tile)
desc: The current lab default. The tile answers nothing the content asks, so it is wallpaper at small size. It is the starting point every transformation in this round leaves.

name: Standard GPS dashboard (fullscreen + floating cards)
desc: Explicitly what the brief forbids. Cards float without binding to geometry, the map becomes backdrop, and it is indistinguishable from any fleet GPS product.

name: Map left + white panel right
desc: The default split. The panel repeats the strip and the map shows sea and Spain. Nothing binds the two halves.

name: A3 · Full route + bottom journey strip (leaders bind strip to geometry)
desc: The strip stays a strip (distance-true) and dashed leaders bind each station to its geographic place, so neither representation is sacrificed. Calm and clearly FleetOS.

name: A4 · Route with edge timeline (time runs UP the right edge, with travel)
desc: Time runs up because the truck travels north (a first draft with time running down crossed every leader). Portugal's N–S shape lets the vertical time axis and the route share direction. Leaders from hours to places make time-geography one reading, which no GPS dashboard does.

name: A2 · Corridor fullscreen (geography unrolled, tracks above and below)
desc: Strong (Round 1 R-03), but as a fullscreen it is a chart with a map texture. Better as the target of a transition (A3 → A2) than as a destination.

name: A5 · Spatial object inspector (truck docked to its marker, dark)
desc: The technical object survives the jump to fullscreen and points at itself on the map. Range is drawn on the route (fuel → km), so geography answers a vehicle question.

name: A6 · Tactical multi-resource (who can reach J-4223's pickup)
desc: The right question and a good brushing interaction, but the rings are crow-flies circles posing as drive time, which is misleading. Real isochrones are needed before this is a KEEP.

name: A7 · Restriction segment with section cutout (detail A)
desc: Borrows the CAD 'detail A' callout. The section of the physical fact (clearance) is bound to the exact place on the street map. Map, logic and object are all native, with no panel.

name: A8 · Stop at street level (Santarém service area)
desc: Street detail is real (OSM) and the clock ring at the stop is a good idea, but we don't own service-area layouts, so 'where it parks' is still a promise. Keep the ring idea.

name: A8 · Delivery stop at street level (Campanhã) with final approach
desc: The final approach is where geography matters most. Minute ticks drawn along the street line and the underpass annotated in place make it a strong local map.

name: A1 · Portrait country spine + ledger (operation)
desc: The Round 1 winner on real coastline. Portugal-native, no wasted width, and rows and trucks are bound by leaders.

name: A1-dark · Night operation spine
desc: Calm dark mode works and the embers are legible, but it's a re-skin of A1, not a new spatial idea. Keep as the tone variant.

name: Instrument frame (edge-mounted gauges around a full map)
desc: A cockpit frame. Side gauges detached from geometry are the standard GPS-dashboard reflex in disguise. Only the bottom strip earns its edge.

name: Map cutout inside a document-like page
desc: The principle (map shrinks to the decision region) is right and goes into the rules; the shaped clip is a stylistic flourish that would age badly.

name: Map-free: document anchor with a locator line
desc: The rule (the map leaves when it stops answering) is essential, but the screen itself is just a document stage. It's recorded as a prominence rule, not a composition.

name: Map as top band, Marey below (map changes axis to share km)
desc: The idea is right (the map adopts the plane's axis), but the Marey here plots km vertically, so the alignment is only half real. Flip the Marey axes before using it.

name: Route strip integrated into the line (hour ticks on geometry)
desc: Hour ticks on the road are honest and cheap, but they crowd quickly and need careful thinning. A layer of A3, not a destination.

name: Technical object + geography: cargo leaves at each stop
desc: The load plan splitting onto the map is a lovely continuity move, but the geography adds little to 'Coimbra first'. Better as a motion than as a destination.

name: Causal rule + geography (conditions attached to where they are true)
desc: Spatially anchoring the time condition at the crossing is powerful, but anchoring vehicle facts at the truck position is arbitrary (they aren't spatial). A hybrid: spatial conditions on the map, physical ones on the object.

name: Corridor zoom (Lisboa–Leiria) with legal remainder + day crossing the map
desc: D-05 (legal → km) finally at the right scale on real geography. The day ribbon crossing the map keeps time present without a panel. Best fullscreen Driver candidate.

name: Two stops compared side-by-side at street scale
desc: Twin maps at equal scale sound fair, but the deciding facts aren't spatial and one side lacks data. It looks rigorous and answers nothing.

name: Restriction regional fullscreen (IP3) with time band crossing the map
desc: Better than Round 1's X-07 thanks to the time band, but still mostly empty land. It earns fullscreen only at night with several trucks affected.

name: Operation brushing (hover radius highlights everything near the cursor)
desc: Brushing is a genuine spatial query (kepler.gl), but it's an interaction, not a composition. Keep it as a behaviour of A1.

name: Driver → +Route → +Restriction → map dominant → fullscreen → click Truck (anchor switch)
desc: The reference transformation. Each step adds one lens and the geometry grows only when the question becomes spatial. On anchor switch the map holds still and only the docked object and the line styling change.

name: Transport → Route focus → Stop focus → local zoom → compare two stops → Esc restores
desc: The bottom strip survives every zoom by re-scoping its km range, a great continuity rule. Esc restores the exact A3 geometry. The twin-stop step is the weakest.

name: Truck → Restriction → affected segment → physical clearance → back to map
desc: Object continuity is complete: the drawing becomes the marker and returns as the portal view. Logic collapses into a map annotation instead of a panel. Best normal↔spatial transition.

name: Operation → hover transport → select → route grows, others fade → Driver lens → legal corridor
desc: Isolate-by-ghosting (CAD) keeps context without clutter, and the selected row becoming the headline is clean continuity. The camera reframe during layout movement explains the change.

name: Map disappears: Route fullscreen → Documents → locator line → document stage
desc: Demonstrates the disappearance rule, but the intermediate split frame is a generic map-plus-document layout. The rule survives; the sequence doesn't.

name: Map changes axis: landscape route → portrait spine → corridor band
desc: Axis change is right, but the straightening step cannot be shown honestly with a camera move (it needs a geometric morph). The frames read as cuts. Needs a real morph implementation to judge.

name: Map expands while the layout collapses
desc: The map grows from the right column to fullscreen while the day ribbon compresses into the left edge strip. Both move on the same curve, so space visibly flows from content to geography.

name: Camera reframes during layout movement
desc: Portrait → landscape → corridor: the camera's fit changes while the frame changes, keeping the selected truck at the same reading position. The portrait→landscape reframe jumps too far: the selected truck does not keep its reading position. It needs an anchored camera (keep the selected object fixed on screen).

name: Driver timeline compresses into an edge strip
desc: The horizontal day ribbon becomes a vertical edge timeline; 'now' and the 10:50 wall stay visible throughout.

name: Truck object moves from technical canvas to map marker
desc: The drawing shrinks and fades into its marker position while the map grows behind it; object continuity explained by motion.

name: Restriction logic collapses into a map annotation
desc: The full logic tree folds into a compact chip at the map edge and the physical detail returns as a small portal inset. The logic tree crossfades into the chip rather than folding into it, so the motion doesn't yet explain the collapse. It needs a real morph of the five conditions.

name: Route axis becomes a geographic corridor
desc: Landscape → portrait → straightened corridor. Currently a cut, not a morph: the honest version needs path interpolation.

name: Anchor changes while the map stays open
desc: Driver → Truck: the map doesn't move; line styling switches from legal (amber) to fuel (blue), and the truck drawing docks with a leader.

name: Esc restores the prior geometry exactly
desc: Route → street zoom → Esc. The camera and the strip return to the identical A3 state (same fit, same strip scale).

name: Day horizon (12-hour arc around now)
desc: Striking and instantly 'not a fleet tool'. The arc centres 'now' so past and future are symmetric and the legal wall cuts the horizon like a sunset line. It's hard to read durations on an arc, though, and it only shows ±6h.

name: The number (sparse)
desc: One number, one place, one consequence. It survives any screen size and reads from across a room. A perfect lock-screen and attention state.

name: Week as terrain (ridgelines)
desc: Fourteen days as stacked ridgelines reveal rhythm (early starts, long Fridays) in one glance. Legal thresholds become horizon lines. Beautiful, but exact values need hover.

name: Commitments ledger (who he owes what)
desc: A new mental model (promises, not timelines) and the copy is excellent, but visually it's a list of sentences. Keep the framing as language across FleetOS, not as a screen.

name: Legal reach envelope (time × km cone)
desc: Evolves Round 2's C-03 into a pure instrument: the cone of legally reachable positions, with the plan inside it and the stop places as horizontal lines. The best legality representation so far.

name: Calendar landscape (isometric month)
desc: Pretty isometric blocks, but occlusion hides the very days you need, and heights are unreadable in perspective. Concept-art toy.

name: Qualifications as runways (validity vs assignments)
desc: Each qualification is a runway that ends at expiry; planned transports are aircraft that must land before the end. 'J-4302 runs off the CQM runway' is instantly understood, and it scales to 40 drivers as rows.

name: Cluster (automotive instrument, dark)
desc: Beautiful cab HMI, wrong user. A dispatcher reading three dials is skeuomorphism, and it can't show 40 drivers.

name: The day drawn as the road
desc: The real road is unrolled and coloured by what the driver is doing on it: driving, pause, unloading. Clock times are milestones on the asphalt, and the legal wall is a line across the road. Time and space are literally one object.

name: Reassignment duel (two names, one transport)
desc: Poster-scale decision clarity, but it only works for two candidates and hides the time geometry that justifies the choice. Pair it with a time comparison.

name: 30-day activity barcode (history)
desc: Excellent density and anomaly pop-out, but it's a history view that is rarely opened. It belongs as a strip inside the Driver screen.

name: Where he has been (spatial week traces)
desc: The portrait country with five days of traces shows familiarity and home base, which is useful for reassignment ('he knows the VCI'). As a daily screen, though, it answers a rare question.

name: String chart (Ibry/Marey) with gates and barriers
desc: The 150-year-old railway answer. Windows are gates the line must pass through, restrictions are hatched barriers in km×time, slack is a gap you can measure, and a second line shows the alternative. It scales to many transports on one corridor.

name: Rail diagram (octilinear schematic with branch)
desc: Beck's rules applied to a road trip: 45° geometry, stations evenly spaced by importance, and the alternative as a branch line. Restrictions are 'closed stations'. Instantly legible and unmistakably distinctive, a signature candidate.

name: Diagonal journey (editorial)
desc: A gorgeous diagonal that holds one transport and wastes half the canvas. Concept art.

name: Timetable (typographic, dense)
desc: A railway timetable: stops as rows, planned / predicted / alternative / window as columns, with deviations in red only. Zero chart literacy needed and extremely dense. It is the 'Bloomberg' of routes.

name: Trajectory field (all plausible futures)
desc: Forty plausible futures (speed and pause variations) fan from 'now'. Windows are gates, and the share of lines passing each gate is the confidence. Honest about uncertainty and visually powerful, but it needs a real probabilistic model behind it.

name: Split stage: current vs alternative
desc: Two unrolled corridors at the same km scale, top and bottom, with the differences as a seam of deltas between them. A clear comparison, but corridor strips are thin for so much width.

name: Route as a folded paper strip (accordion)
desc: The folded-map metaphor is charming, but the folds distort distance and hide information at every crease. It's a beautiful object and a bad instrument.

name: Fuel tube (depletion as a physical tank along the road)
desc: A horizontal tube whose fill drains along km and refills at Santarém. The reserve is a red floor, and anyone gets it. It is a single-variable view, though: a layer, not a route screen.

name: Geographic corridor + stacked strata (geology section)
desc: Calm and dense, but km-aligned strata are a refinement of Round 1's console, not a new direction. It becomes a layer of the winner.

name: Editorial route narrative (path through text)
desc: The editorial narrative is lovely for a client deck but useless while the truck is moving. Not a FleetOS screen.

name: Gates in sequence (multi-stop execution, exception-first)
desc: Great exception scan at poster scale, but stripping out time and space makes it a summary, not a route instrument.

name: Portrait route on Natural Earth + km column
desc: A refined Round 3 spatial state on real coastline, with a km column aligned by latitude. Good, but not new, and it doesn't stop anyone.

name: Engineering drawing sheet (three views + title block)
desc: The vehicle as a real drawing sheet: side elevation, front, top plan and a title block (registration, revision, assignment). The revision table is the change history and detail callouts point at the open facts. Engineers and dispatchers both recognise it at once.

name: Section through the trailer (load cutaway + centre of gravity)
desc: Physically correct and beautiful, but centre of gravity is a niche question for dispatch. It's a drawing layer, not a screen.

name: Exploded combination (parts with states)
desc: Cleaner than Round 1's V-11: the tractor, fifth wheel, trailer and axle groups float apart on one axis, each with its state. Useful for 'which part is the problem', but a heavy drawing for a simple answer.

name: From below (axles, tyres, brakes)
desc: An underside plan nobody shows: each tyre carries tread depth, each axle its load and brake state. Perfect for the workshop, too specialised for dispatch.

name: Silhouette against every gate (front overlays)
desc: The truck's front silhouette is overlaid on the outlines of every structure on its route, aligned at the road, like a key in many locks. The tightest fit pops out without reading.

name: The tank (fuel as a physical vessel)
desc: A single tank cross-section, litres as liquid, range as a rod measured against the road ahead. Immediately clear, but a one-variable screen.

name: Maintenance aligned to the machine
desc: Workshop-grade and well aligned, but the labels collide with the drawing at desk size. Needs the sheet format of ZV-01.

name: Coupling fan (which trailer fits the tractor)
desc: Trailers fanning around the fifth wheel like keys on a ring is a memorable image, but the rotations make comparison impossible. Visually strong, operationally unclear.

name: Plate and one line (sparse)
desc: Says nothing a list row couldn't. Calm is not the same as useful.

name: Mass over distance (the truck lightens along the road)
desc: A mass-over-km area chart whose top edge is drawn as the trailer roofline: 27.6 t until Coimbra, a step down to 25 t, then a final drop. Structures with mass limits sit on the same axis. A rare honest weight view.

name: Commitment structure (who promised what, depends on what)
desc: A structurally brilliant idea (promises rest on resources), but the links clutter quickly. It needs a focus mode before it's a screen.

name: Live execution (one bar, one sentence)
desc: Superbly clear, but thin: once the bar repeats it is O-01's micro-journey row. A state, not a screen.

name: Exception-first (only what deviates)
desc: ISA-101 philosophy applied: everything nominal is grey, and only deviations get magnitude bars against their tolerance. The screen is mostly calm, and that calm is information.

name: Cargo movement (pallets flowing through places and time)
desc: Every pallet is a square flowing left to right through time, splitting at Coimbra and exiting at Porto. Gorgeous and tangible, but for 24 pallets it's mostly repetition, and it doesn't scale to groupage.

name: People · equipment · places (three bands over time)
desc: Places run along the middle band; people above and equipment below show who and what is bound to each leg. It shows hand-overs (a trailer swap, a driver change) as breaks in the band. Good for multi-leg transports, overkill for single-driver runs.

name: Plan lineage (revisions as stacked plans)
desc: Seven revisions of the plan drawn as offset journey strips. What changed between each pair is marked at the km where it changed, so you see the plan's evolution as geology. Strong for audit, rare need.

name: Case file (the transport as a physical dossier)
desc: The manila case file is charming, but its tabs bring back exactly the tab structure this round was told to abandon.

name: Next decision as a fork (decision tree with consequences)
desc: The current state sits on the left and the decision branches to the right with each branch's consequences drawn to the end of the day (arrival times, legality, cost). The recommended branch is inked. It makes the next decision a visible fork.

name: Editorial front page of a transport
desc: Duplicates ZO-06 at lower value. One editorial front page is enough, and it belongs at operation level.

name: The sheet at reading scale with margin annotations
desc: The best 'document at reading scale', but it evolves Round 1's F-03 rather than breaking new ground. It becomes part of the documents winner.

name: Signature relay (the paper travels through hands)
desc: The document is drawn as it physically travels: Faro hands it signed, the driver carries it, Coimbra and Porto will stamp it. Each hand-over is a stamp on a time axis. It turns 'signature status' into a relay race anyone can read.

name: Version lineage (git graph of revisions)
desc: Clear, scalable and familiar, but a git graph is borrowed language with little FleetOS character. Good as a detail view.

name: Documents attached to cargo (each pallet carries its paper)
desc: Paper tags tied to the pallet groups in the load plan: the CMR line for Coimbra hangs on the six pallets near the doors. A clever physical binding, but documents rarely map one-to-one to pallets.

name: Onion skin (snapshot over current)
desc: Onion skin is clever in theory; in practice two overlapping forms are illegible below 4K.

name: Receipt tape (documents printed by events)
desc: Events on the transport timeline print paper receipts that hang below the moment they were produced (load, issue, toll, refuel, POD), so documents become evidence of events. A distinctive, honest model that scales by scrolling time.

name: Document table (reference)
desc: Included deliberately as the baseline every other study must beat. It's a file table with status pills, and it fails on every FleetOS value except listability.

name: Forbidden regions (km × time) for all transports on the corridor
desc: Restrictions are forbidden rectangles in a shared space-time plane and every transport crossing the corridor is a string. A conflict is a string entering a rectangle. One picture serves the whole operation.

name: Decision tree with fact provenance (vertical)
desc: Clean and correct, but a vertical tree spends a whole screen on four conditions. It folds into the two-futures winner.

name: Route through the restricted ring (street level)
desc: Real Porto streets, the ring hatched and the route's 2.8 km inside it highlighted. Clear and honest, but it's Round 3's G-09 without the section bubble, so nothing new.

name: Two futures of a missing fact
desc: The screen splits on the unknown: if the axle is < 1.1 m (left) the transport is untouched; if ≥ 1.1 m (right) these transports and these hours are affected. Missing data becomes a visible bet with a price, a new and honest pattern.

name: The law, typeset, with clauses bound to facts
desc: The regulation article set like a printed page, with clauses underlined and each tied by a margin leader to the fact that satisfies it. Excellent evidence and trust, but slow to read, so it's a fold-out, not a main screen.

name: Gate gallery (front elevations through every structure)
desc: Round 2's C-15 refined. Still the clearest physical restriction picture, but it duplicates the vehicle domain's ZV-05.

name: Restriction register (reference)
desc: Baseline included on purpose: a rule list without when, where or for whom. Every study above beats it.

name: Day board with restriction bands (temporal operation)
desc: Still the dispatch backbone, but it's Round 1's O-03 cleaned. Necessary infrastructure, not a new idea.

name: Latitude metro (country as parallel lines)
desc: Portugal's latitude is the shared axis and transports are parallel metro lines, with cities as transfer bands. Nothing in fleet software looks like this, yet it's immediately readable for a N–S country.

name: Attention stream (typography only, ranked)
desc: Round 1's O-07, purer: four sentences ranked by time-to-consequence, each with its countdown in the margin. The calmest possible command centre, and the right landing state.

name: Dispatch wall (the whole day, ultra-dense)
desc: A 'Bloomberg' wall where every transport is one line with micro-journey, legal clock, fuel, documents and the next event as glyph columns, built for a 4K wall screen. Powerful at scale, intimidating at desk size.

name: Resource pairing (drivers ⇄ trucks ⇄ transports)
desc: Three columns of resources with arcs pairing them for today. Unpaired resources dangle, so idle capacity and orphan transports are visible at once. A good assignment overview, but crossing arcs get messy past 20.

name: Newspaper front page of the operation
desc: The operation as the morning paper: headline, three stories, a portrait map figure and the weather box as road conditions. Perfect for shift handover, too static for live work.

name: Slack skyline (comparison landscape)
desc: Each transport is a tower whose height is minutes of slack to its tightest commitment; towers below ground are already late. The skyline ranks the operation's risk at a glance. Strong, but it hides why.

name: Portrait country + exceptions only (ISA-101 map)
desc: A Natural Earth portrait with all routes in grey; only exceptions get ink and a label bound to their location. Calm when calm, loud only where needed. The geographic home screen.

name: Commitments clock (all windows of the day on one ring)
desc: A 24h ring with every delivery window as an arc is pretty, but it collapses which transport owns which window, and circular time again loses to linear. Rejected.

name: Driver · the day drawn as the road (pass 1)
desc: Adds the number (0:45) as the anchor, km ticks on the asphalt and the four legal counters as hairline gauges. The road keeps all the meaning while the counters sit quietly at the bottom.

name: Driver · the day drawn as the road (pass 2)
desc: Adds lay-bys off the road as the real pause candidates (capacity, fuel, out-of-limit), a seven-day barcode for rhythm, and a quieter type scale. The full legal and spatial answer on one canvas with no panel. Signature screen.

name: Route · string chart (pass 1)
desc: Cleaner grid (every other hour), gates as brackets, barriers hatched, a single dashed alternative, slack values on the gates, and the pause as a physical block. A railway instrument without chart-junk.

name: Route · string chart + real corridor on its axis (pass 2)
desc: Applies the MBTA lesson (string charts need a map beside them) the Portugal way. The real corridor, unrolled vertically, shares the chart's km axis, so geography and time-distance are read on one line of sight. Signature screen.

name: Vehicle · drawing sheet (pass 1)
desc: Proper sheet grid references, four numbered views (elevation, front, detail A, load plan), a revision table that is the vehicle's history, and a title block that is its identity. The open fact lives in a detail callout.

name: Vehicle · drawing sheet with service conditions (pass 2)
desc: The sheet gains a 'service conditions' band (the next 274 km with gates, fuel and mass), so the machine meets its journey without leaving the drawing language. Signature screen.

name: Transport · the next decision as a fork in time (pass 1)
desc: Branches now live on a real time axis, so each consequence (pause, legality, Coimbra, Porto, fuel) is placed when it happens, with windows and the legal wall as vertical references. The fork becomes measurable.

name: Transport · fork + exceptions margin (pass 2)
desc: A left margin lists the transport's state in ISA-101 style (normal in grey, exceptions in colour), so the fork is read in context. One screen holds state, decision and consequences. Signature screen.

name: Documents · receipts of events + the selected sheet (pass 1)
desc: The receipt tape becomes the index and the selected receipt (CMR rev. 7) opens at reading scale below with margin notes. Event → paper → content in one vertical reading.

name: Documents · receipts + signature stamps + sheet (pass 2)
desc: Signature stamps sit above the tape on the same time axis (done = blue ink, pending = dashed), so the relay (ZF-02) and the receipts (ZF-06) merge into one paper timeline over the open sheet. Signature screen.

name: Restriction · two futures of a missing fact (pass 1)
desc: Each future gets its own small space-time plane showing which transports would hit the barrier, and the missing measurement is drawn at the axle in the centre. The bet, its price and the task are all visible.

name: Restriction · two futures + the rule path (pass 2)
desc: A thin rule path across the top shows which conditions are known (inked) and which one splits the world (dashed), then forks into the two futures. Logic, consequence, physical fact and action, with no panel. Signature screen.

name: Operation · latitude metro, exceptions in ink (pass 1)
desc: Healthy lines recede to grey and only exceptions keep ink and a one-line note at the head of their line (ISA-101). The country shape still organises everything.

name: Operation · latitude metro + attention rail (pass 2)
desc: Adds ETA ticks at line ends, the VCI barrier as a latitude band across all lines, and a right rail with the four decisions ranked by time-to-consequence. Geography, time and attention on one surface. Signature screen.

name: Operation · base / attention · Attention sentences + portrait figure
desc: The calmest home possible. Ranked sentences carry the decisions, inline actions sit inside each sentence, and the portrait map is a figure that confirms geography without competing.

name: Operation · base / attention · Latitude metro + attention rail
desc: The Round 4 signature survives inside a product. The floating rail stays out of the way, and the attention rail narrows or moves under the metro at 1199. Distinctive and legible.

name: Operation · base / attention · Ledger + portrait map + action strip
desc: The most implementable and scalable, and the closest to a classic tool. The micro-journey rows keep it FleetOS, but the three-column skeleton is generic and the map column is half wallpaper.

name: Operation · Driver population · Drivers as day ribbons (edge nav)
desc: Every driver on one clock with legal state in the row, and a sentence header. Edge navigation reads as a ruler and disappears into the margin. Dense and calm, it scales to 40.

name: Operation · Fleet population · Fleet rows with load silhouettes
desc: Silhouettes show load and state at a glance, with location and next maintenance in each row. Good, but repeated silhouettes become texture past 15 rows. Needs a compact glyph mode.

name: Operation · Routes population · Portrait country, exceptions bound by leaders
desc: ISA-101 geography: grey routes, ink only on exceptions, with labels flowing to a right gutter by leader lines. No panel and no landscape waste.

name: Operation · Restrictions population · Forbidden regions plane + rule column
desc: All restrictions as space-time barriers with every transport as a string, plus a left column that names each rule and its exposure. The operation-wide restriction view.

name: Driver · Today · Number + road + gauges
desc: The Round 4 signature in a real shell. The number anchors, the road carries time and place, and the gauges sit in the footer zone. Reflows from a stacked 1199 to a 1920 with week context.

name: Driver · Today · Ribbon instrument + legal bands + bottom stops
desc: Clear and implementable: chip anchor, ruler lenses, ribbon with legal bands and an attached action at the pause. But it's the Round 1 D-01 page with a rail, missing the road's distinctiveness.

name: Driver · Today · Identity column + time spine with lens rows
desc: Lenses are rows added to one shared clock (activity, legality, stops, documents, vehicle), so adding context never creates a new page. The identity column stays fixed. The most dynamic-friendly grammar.

name: Driver · Legality · Legal reach cone as the instrument
desc: The cone holds the full legal answer, and the chip anchor plus ruler lenses keep identity without stealing scale. Edge actions stay out of the instrument. It needs a one-time explanation.

name: Driver · Driver + Truck · Person ⇄ machine joints on the drawing
desc: Compatibility joints between the person card and the drawing work. The receding crumb is elegant, but the joints still read as a diagram (Round 1's D-04 problem) once surrounded by UI.

name: Driver · Driver + Route · Legal corridor on real geography + day crossing
desc: Round 3's best Driver spatial state inside the shell. The floating rail recedes, the day ribbon crosses the map as a band, and the confirm action is attached to Santarém on the map.

name: Driver · Driver + Restriction · Sentence + rule path + exposure plane
desc: Honest and readable: the sentence, the conditions path and the driver's crossing on a small plane. But the driver anchor feels incidental; this belongs to the restriction anchor.

name: Driver · dense multi-context · Commitments + instrument + map + papers
desc: Everything at once works for a power user at 1920. At 1440 the four regions compete and the road loses its scale. Density is achieved, distinctiveness drops.

name: Truck · Load · Elevation + plan hero, unload order, docked inset
desc: The machine is the page. The elevation and plan are aligned, the unload order is drawn to the doors, and the action sits at the doors. A tiny docked inset says where without a map region.

name: Truck · Technical · Drawing sheet as the full page
desc: The drawing sheet is FleetOS's most distinctive vehicle state and reads as a complete product state. Lower dynamic potential: it's a document, not a workspace.

name: Truck · Maintenance · Component lifelines hung from the drawing
desc: Wear aligned to component position is right, but labels fight the drawing at 1440. It works at 1920 or with the sheet format.

name: Truck · Truck + Restriction · Front silhouette vs gates + detail cutout
desc: The physical answer is centred, the gate outlines overlay the silhouette, and a circular street cutout says where the tightest gate is. Instantly understood.

name: Truck · Truck + Route · Object docked to its marker on a dark corridor
desc: Beautiful, and the docked drawing keeps continuity. But dark tone for a daytime question breaks the 'grey is normal' language, so it's better as the paper variant.

name: Transport · Narrative · Front page of the transport
desc: In a real shell the front page reads like a briefing, ideal for handover or client view. It's static, though: once things move, an editorial layout ages in minutes.

name: Transport · Execution · Decision fork + ISA-101 margin
desc: The Round 4 signature in a shell: a rail, a grey-normal margin and the fork on time. The 'execution' state has one obvious next action, attached to the recommended branch. Best execution layout.

name: Transport · Team · People · equipment · places bands
desc: Bands show who and what is bound to each leg and make hand-overs visible. A good team view for multi-leg work, too heavy for single-driver transports.

name: Transport · Documents · Paper timeline over the open sheet
desc: Receipts on the top timeline, stamps above it, and the selected sheet at reading scale below. The documents of a transport finally read as evidence of events. Survives inside the shell.

name: Transport · Revision · Plan lineage + reissue proposal bar
desc: The proposal bar works here: revisions stack as plans, the pending change appears as rev. 8 drawn dashed, and the dark bar states the consequence. The clearest editing state in the set.

name: Transport · dense · Strip + string chart + map + papers + strip actions
desc: It holds everything a power user wants, but at 1440 the string chart is cramped and the map column is decorative. Better as a 1920-only mode.

name: Route · time–distance · String chart + vertical corridor
desc: The strongest route state in context. The corridor column and the chart share the km axis, and the alternative's action sits on its dashed line. Reflows: at 1199 the corridor narrows to a ribbon; at 1920 a stop column appears.

name: Route · corridor · Unrolled corridor + km strata
desc: The geology-section route as a full product state: the corridor band on top and strata for road, legality, fuel, restrictions and cargo. Edge nav and one attached action. Calm, dense, distinctive.

name: Route · map-dominant · Full route + bottom strip bound by leaders
desc: Round 3's A3 archetype holds up in the shell: floating rail, edge actions and a distance-true strip bound to the geography. The most implementable spatial state.

name: Route · alternative comparison · Two strings + delta ledger + proposal
desc: Comparison as geometry: current and alternative strings on one chart, a delta ledger beside it, and the proposal bar for 'adopt alternative'. Clear recommendation and consequence.

name: Route · stop focus · Street approach + minute ticks + local strip
desc: Street-level OSM, the final approach with minute ticks, the underpass marked in place, and a strip re-scoped to the last 36 km. The local stop state the product never had.

name: Documents · dossier · Sheet centre stage + margin notes + tape
desc: A strong reading experience, but the dossier is really W-24 with the timeline compressed. Two document layouts are one too many.

name: Documents · diff · Two sheets, marks on the fields, cause in the margin
desc: The sheets themselves are the interface: diff marks on the fields and the cause written in the margin. The receding crumb gives the whole width to paper.

name: Documents · issue / reissue · Cause → sheet → consequence + proposal
desc: Reissue reads left to right (change, affected field, consequences) and the proposal bar makes it a single, explicit commitment. The editing grammar for every document.

name: Restrictions · applicability · Verdict sentence + conditions path + evidence fold
desc: Very clear and cheap to build, but it is a sentence and a row of boxes. It needs the two-futures or plane to earn its screen.

name: Restrictions · missing fact · Axle gap hero + two futures
desc: The missing fact is drawn where it lives (the axle), with the world split on it and priced. The task is attached to the drawing. Distinctive and actionable.

name: Restrictions · route impact · Barrier on the plane + affected rows
desc: Solid, but a single-restriction variant of W-07. Keep W-07 and filter it by restriction instead of a separate layout.

name: Restrictions · spatial segment · Street segment + detail-A cutout + logic chip
desc: Round 3's G-09 holds in the shell: the ring at street level, the physical section in a CAD bubble, and the logic as a small chip. No panel, all bound to the place.

name: Inbox · triage what needs me
desc: Every office worker already knows this. The alerts are the 'emails'; open one and act with big buttons. Lowest learning curve. Email-style three panes: folders, alert list, reading pane

group: Trello-like · DM Sans · purple · grey canvas
name: Board · transports by stage
desc: Planning becomes moving cards. Status is position, not a label. Very easy to explain to new staff. Kanban columns, drag cards between stages

group: Airtable-like · IBM Plex Sans · green · dense grid
name: Grid · everything in one sheet
desc: Office workers live in Excel. Sortable, filterable, editable in place, exportable. Power without training. Spreadsheet with filters, grouping, coloured pills, inline edit

name: Calendar · who drives when
desc: Scheduling in the tool everybody already uses for meetings. Conflicts are overlaps; free time is white space. Week calendar, drivers as coloured events; click empty slot to assign

group: MS-Project-like · Source Sans 3 · orange · toolbar ribbon
name: Gantt · plan the week
desc: Planners see utilisation and gaps across the week; drag a transport to another truck. Familiar to anyone who used Project. Resource rows (trucks) × days, bars draggable, ribbon toolbar

name: Dark list · keyboard-first
desc: For the fast dispatcher who lives on the keyboard: ⌘K to do anything, J/K to move, single-key actions shown in rows. Sidebar + list with keyboard shortcuts + command palette

name: Live map · tap a truck
desc: Feels like apps everyone uses on the phone. Answers 'where is it' instantly; detail slides in with one tap. Full map, floating list panel, big rounded detail sheet

name: Assistant · ask in plain words
desc: No menus to learn: 'who can take J-4218?' Answers carry the action buttons. Great for occasional users and managers. Chat with the operation; answers come as small tables and buttons

group: Office dashboard · Work Sans · navy + yellow
name: Today · tiles + to-do
desc: The manager's morning screen: how many, what's late, what to do. Readable from across the office. Big number tiles, a to-do list, today's deliveries table

group: Classic business app · Inter · slate · forms
name: Record · transport form
desc: Exactly how invoices and orders look in every ERP — editable fields, save, history. Zero surprise for back-office staff. Header with status + actions, tabs, two-column fields, activity log

name: Checklist · today's run sheet
desc: Dispatch as a checklist: things tick themselves when they happen; you only act on unchecked items with a red dot. Time-ordered task list per transport with progress and big ticks

name: Board · high contrast
desc: For the screen on the office wall: readable from 6 m, no hover, no clutter. Problems in yellow, the rest in white on black. Giant type wallboard for the depot screen

group: Touch-first · Nunito Sans · orange · huge targets
name: Touch · yard tablet
desc: For the yard or cais on a tablet: gloves-friendly buttons, one decision per screen, no tiny text. Two panes with 64px rows and thumb-sized buttons

group: Editorial print · Source Serif 4 · black · A4 rhythm
name: Report · daily summary for the boss
desc: Some people want a page, not an app: emailed at 08:00 or printed for the morning meeting. Same data, zero interface. One readable page: summary, exceptions, table, signatures

group: Guided flow · Plus Jakarta Sans · cyan · stepper
name: Wizard · assign a driver in 3 steps
desc: For rare or risky tasks: the tool walks you through, ranks the options, and shows the consequences before you confirm. Stepper with choice cards, recommendation badge, summary before confirm
